title: The End of Apps — Kitze, Sizzy.co

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on Kitze's personal journey through productivity apps and AI agent products, focusing on UX, collaboration patterns, and product vision rather than agent architecture internals. The entire talk is about individual assistant and consumer productivity use cases, from to-do apps to personal multi-agent systems. Wolfer is described as an in-progress personal experiment built on Codex, not a production-deployed system. Assumes familiarity with Claude Code, MCP, and self-hosting but remains accessible to a general AI engineer audience. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer channel. Multiple direct transcript excerpts consistently support the product and UX framing throughout the talk.

summary: Kitze opens his 34th-birthday AI Engineer talk, mentioning Tinker Club. He traces a personal history from childhood to-do lists at age 10 through multiple unfinished apps — 'to do do it,' 'Better,' and 'Benji' (~60 features, named after his dog) — none of which shipped due to ADHD-driven feature creep and marketing avoidance. A Benji voice-to-API feature went viral but was never productized. After ChatGPT plugins briefly convinced him SaaS was dead, he tried personal skills on Claude Code but found coding and personal skill mixing confusing. Discovering Pete's Claude bot via WhatsApp/Telegram was his breakthrough; he went 'full lobster mode' in the OpenClaw community, self-hosting on NAS, Nextcloud, and markdown, switching to Android for richer agent control. He found ~90% of cited OpenClaw use cases already work with Claude Code or Codex, and that single-agent one-on-one chat is inadequate for multi-context delegation. He tried spreading across five Discords with specialized agents, but community enthusiasm waned as meetups shrank to ~5 people. Discord and Telegram are fundamentally unsuited as Life OS interfaces. He sees two futures competing: custom agents for tinkerers only, and cloud agents too nerfed for tinkerers but suitable for the masses. He is building 'Wolfer,' a personal multi-agent orchestration app using nested topics instead of memory systems. He predicts AI's role will invert: agents will ingest all life data and prompt humans with the next task. Most consumer apps will become unnecessary as a futuristic OS emerges; a small set of specialist apps (color grading, music making) will survive. Normies will chat to their computers with UI generating on the fly. He speculates Apple could win because local models are improving rapidly, and a local Siri with tool capabilities across installed apps would offer privacy, zero credits, and on-device automation — a vision already partially realized by Google Pixel's background app actions. He closes by acknowledging he is over time and invites discussion.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and personal productivity history
sections.summary: Kitze introduces himself on his 34th birthday, mentions Tinker Club, and frames the talk around the past, present, and future of productivity and personal agents. He recounts childhood to-do lists at age 10, dissatisfaction with to-do apps, using Android Tasker with text files for contextual reminders, and Google Home plus IFTTT for voice-captured tasks.

sections.title: Building Benji and feature creep
sections.summary: Kitze walks through prior apps — 'to do do it,' 'Better,' and 'Benji' (~60 features). ADHD-driven feature creep and marketing avoidance kept Benji unfinished for 3-4 years. A voice-to-API feature went viral but was never productized; others monetized single features into multi-million businesses.

sections.title: ChatGPT moment and Claude Code skills
sections.summary: Kitze recalls declaring SaaS dead to his wife after ChatGPT plugins. He loaded personal skills onto Claude Code but found mixing coding and personal skills confusing, and sought a non-terminal interface for a broader personal assistant.

sections.title: Claude bot and lobster mode
sections.summary: Discovering Pete's Claude bot via WhatsApp/Telegram was Kitze's breakthrough. He went 'full lobster mode' in the OpenClaw community and committed to owning his assistant, files, and memory locally.

sections.title: Self-hosting and questioning packaged agents
sections.summary: Kitze migrated data to local NAS, Nextcloud, and markdown, and switched to Android for richer agent control. He found ~90% of OpenClaw use cases already work with Claude Code or Codex, and noted single-agent chat is inadequate for multi-context delegation.

sections.title: Multi-agent chaos and community disillusionment
sections.summary: Kitze explains why one agent loaded with all life context is impractical, leading people to use Telegram topics, Discord, and Slack. He created many specialized bots and ended up with five Discords. Community enthusiasm waned — meetups shrank to ~5 people, becoming 'open claw anonymous.' He cites unreliable cron jobs, agents forgetting mid-conversation, and Discord/Telegram being unsuited as Life OS interfaces.

sections.title: Two futures: custom vs cloud agents
sections.summary: Kitze sees two competing futures: custom agents (OpenClaw, Hermes) only viable for tinkerers because they require constant tweaking, and cloud agents (Cohere, OpenAI, Perplexity) too nerfed to satisfy tinkerers but serving the masses. He juggles OpenClaw, Hermes, Paperclip, and Codex daily, reaching for the terminal when agent frustration peaks.

sections.title: Wolfer: building a personal agent app
sections.summary: Kitze began building 'Wolfer,' a personal multi-agent orchestration experiment on top of Codex. Cons include no Telegram/iMessage support, no plugin system, no memory system, no modularity, and ADHD-driven development. Pros include predictable multi-agent UI, nested topics that inject parent descriptions for context instead of memory, workspaces, visible tool calls, predictable cron jobs, agent management UI, and dynamic mentions of documents and knowledge bases.

sections.title: Predicting the inverted future of AI
sections.summary: Kitze argues current computer UX is broken — greeting users with stale updates and tabs. He predicts AI's role will invert: agents will ingest all life data and prompt humans with the next task. He predicts most consumer apps will become unnecessary; non-technical users like grandmothers will accomplish any task through a new futuristic OS.

sections.title: Specialist apps, Apple, and wrap-up
sections.summary: Kitze predicts a small set of specialist apps (color grading, movie making, music making) will survive, while normies will chat to their computers with UI generating on the fly. He speculates Apple could ultimately win because local models are improving rapidly and a local Siri with tool capabilities across installed apps offers privacy, zero credits, and on-device automation. He notes the latest Google Pixel already launches apps in the background to order coffee and perform tasks. He closes by acknowledging he is over time and invites further discussion.
